analysis.one_liner: Imposes a 0.1% tax on purchases of stocks, bonds, and derivatives traded in the U.S.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in July 2023 and died there when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add a 0.1% excise tax on each purchase of a stock, bond, partnership interest, or derivative when the trade happens on a U.S. exchange or involves a U.S. party. It exempts newly issued securities and very short-term debt, and it charges exchanges and brokers with collecting the tax. Money raised through such a tax goes to the Treasury; the bill does not direct it to any specific program. It never left the Ways and Means Committee, so no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the federal government would have collected revenue from high-volume securities trading, and the tax's design concentrates the cost on frequent, large traders rather than on small, occasional investors. Because the bill directs no spending, any benefit to the public would depend on how Congress later chose to use the revenue.

how_it_helps.text: The bill imposes a 0.1% excise tax on each covered purchase of a security, with the buyer's exchange or broker responsible for paying it [S2, S3].

Because the tax is levied on purchases rather than sales and is collected at the exchange or broker level, a small buy-and-hold investor would pay far less over time than a firm that trades millions of times a day [S3].

The bill includes anti-avoidance rules: it taxes transactions by controlled foreign corporations through their U.S. shareholders and directs the Treasury Secretary to write regulations preventing the use of non-U.S. parties to dodge the tax [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the direct cost would fall on buyers of stocks, bonds, and derivatives — overwhelmingly active traders, hedge funds, and other financial firms — with some portion likely passed along to all investors through slightly higher trading costs, including people with 401(k)s and IRAs. Trading volume might also decline somewhat, which would reduce revenue and could affect market liquidity.

drawbacks.text: A transaction tax raises the cost of every trade, and financial firms typically pass some of that cost through to customers, so even long-term savers with retirement accounts would bear a small share [S3].

Economists who have studied similar taxes in other countries warn they can reduce trading volume and shift some trading offshore, which would cut expected revenue — a risk the bill tries to limit by taxing U.S.-linked transactions and directing regulators to write anti-avoidance rules, but cannot fully eliminate [S2, S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A 0.1% tax is small on any single trade but, multiplied across trillions of dollars in annual securities trading, would raise substantial revenue largely from high-frequency and institutional traders. The main honest objections are that some cost reaches ordinary retirement savers through higher trading costs, and that some trading could migrate abroad, shrinking both the revenue and market liquidity. On balance, the incidence is designed to weigh heaviest on the largest, most frequent market participants.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Val Hoyle introduced the Wall Street Tax Act of 2023 on July 25, 2023, with 18 initial cosponsors, all Democrats [S1, S3].
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation [S5].
That referral was the last action of any kind: the bill received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Active traders, hedge funds, and the broader financial industry are better off, because the tax on their transactions never advanced, and no one else is worse off in any concrete way — the bill changed nothing.

industries.industry: Securities traders and investment firms (hedge funds, high-frequency traders, asset managers)
industries.note: A 0.1% tax on every purchase of stocks, bonds, and derivatives would directly cut into the profits of firms that trade at enormous volume, where even a tenth of a percent per trade adds up to large sums. Blocking the bill preserves their current cost structure, which is what happened.

The bill would make exchanges responsible for collecting and remitting the tax, adding compliance work, and a higher cost per trade could reduce overall trading volume on U.S. exchanges. Some trading might shift to foreign venues, though the bill's rules reach transactions involving U.S. parties [S3].

Brokers would collect the tax on off-exchange trades, and some of the cost would likely be passed to customers, including retirement savers, through slightly higher trading costs. For a long-term investor making occasional purchases, the cost on any given trade is tiny — a dollar on a $10,000 stock purchase.
